Planned cesarean section for a singleton term infant in persistent breech presentation decreases short-term perinatal or neonatal mortality as well as a composite outcome of death or serious neonatal morbidity, at the expense of somewhat increased maternal morbidity. A Overall maternal and infant outcomes at two years appear to be no different, except for possibly more medical problems among infants allocated to planned cesarean delivery. B

For preterm breech singletons born at 26-34 weeks of gestation in the setting of preterm labor or preterm rupture of membranes, there is no association between planned cesarean delivery and improved neonatal outcomes. A planned vaginal or planned cesarean mode of delivery may be offered; the decision should be individualized. B .

External cephalic version (ECV) is a safe and effective way to promote cephalic presentation and vaginal delivery, and should be offered to all women with breech presentation starting at 34 to 35 weeks' gestation. A

Moxibustion starting at 33 weeks' gestation may be an alternative to ECV for promoting cephalic presentation for those not wanting to undergo ECV or prior to attempting ECV, but data are conflicting. B
There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine cesarean section for a second twin in breech presentation or for preterm infants. B

background.definition: Breech position is a fetus in longitudinal lie with the cephalic pole in the uterine fundus. Complete breech refers to a fetus with both hips and knees flexed. Incomplete breech (sometimes referred to as single footling or double footling) describes a fetus with one or both hips and knees incompletely flexed so that the foot, or feet, are the presenting part. Frank breech refers to a fetus with hips flexed, but knees extended.

list.listitem: Three percent to 4% of all births, but incidence decreases with increasing gestational age (22%-25% at 28 weeks, 7%-13% at 32 weeks, 5%-7% at 36 weeks, 2.5%-6% at 40 weeks). Frank breech: 48% to 73% Footling breech: 12% to 38% Complete breech: 4.6% to 11.5%
See for variations of breech.
Increased cost at delivery for cesarean section and subsequent longer hospital stay.
Increased short-term maternal morbidity due to cesarean section for delivery.

It appears that even women who undergo successful ECV for breech presentation are at higher risk for cesarean section than women with spontaneous cephalic presentations. In a matched cohort study in the Netherlands, 15% of the 220 women who had successful ECVs were delivered by cesarean section compared to 6% of the 1030 women with spontaneous cephalic presentations.
More or less room for the fetus to move (eg, polyhydramnios, prematurity, macrosomia)
Abnormal placentation (ie, high fundal, marginal or previa)
Uterine malformations (eg, synechiae, Müllerian duct abnormalities, uterine myomata)
Fetal malformations (eg, anencephaly, myotonic dystrophy, hydrocephaly, trisomies)
Pelvic contracture or obstruction
Loss of normal vertical orientation of the uterus thought to be due to laxity of abdominal musculature (ie, grand multiparity)
Fetal lie should be assessed with the prenatal visit starting at 34 to 35 weeks' gestation. B
A low first trimester pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A)-multiple of the median value is associated with breech presentation at term.

Use of moxibustion for breech infants, especially if combined with acupuncture or postural technique, may decrease the need for ECV by promoting version and has minimal risk to mother and infant. B
However, a recent RCT of 328 women with breech presentation did not find moxibustion with acupuncture more effective than inactivated laser (placebo) treatment for correcting breech presentation in the third trimester of pregnancy.
See Other Treatment for additional information on ECV.
Ultrasound is the gold standard for diagnosis of malpresentation. A
Physical examination alone can have poor positive predictive value (PPV). B
In one trial, the sensitivity of the clinical examination for noncephalic presentation was only 70% with a PPV of 55%. B

In one Canadian case series, approximately 8% of breech presentations were undetected until labor; using a vaginal examination to verify fetal presentation (Leopold's maneuvers) did not appear to be more accurate than abdominal palpation alone.

A clinical decision rule was developed and validated to predict the likelihood of success of ECV in 1993. Data from 2018 suggest predictive factors associated with a successful ECV include: use of fenoterol as uterine relaxant, nulliparity, Caucasian ethnicity, gestational age at ECV, Amniotic Fluid Index, type of breech presentation, placental location, breech engagement, possibility to palpate the head and relaxation of the uterus.
Ultrasound is the gold standard test for diagnosis of fetal lie. A
Screen for breech presentation beginning at 34 to 35 weeks using Leopold maneuvers () and vaginal examination. B
Use location of fetal heart tones, vaginal examination, and ultrasound to confirm the fetal position prenatally and at the time of labor.
All women with persistent breech presentation at 37 weeks should be offered ECV as it decreases the rate of noncephalic presentation at birth. A
There is evidence for recommending ECV at 34 to 35 weeks' gestation. B
Routine tocolysis with beta agonists and regional anesthesia are recommended to increase success rates of ECV. B

Planned cesarean section has been shown to decrease mortality and a composite of death or serious neonatal morbidity in term singleton infants in persistent breech presentation at the expense of somewhat increased short-term maternal morbidity and possibly more medical problems among infants allocated to planned cesarean delivery; overall maternal and infant outcomes at 2 years appear to be no different. A

Authors of a Cochrane review of 25 trials concluded that tocolysis with beta agonists for external cephalic version (ECV) increased cephalic presentations in labor (average risk ratio [RR] 1.38; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.03-1.85) and reduced the number of cesarean sections (average RR 0.82; 95% CI, 0.71-0.94). There were insufficient data comparing different tocolytic drugs or on side effects.
In a systematic review, nifedipine was no better than placebo and inferior to terbutaline in success at facilitating ECV.
IV nitroglycerin in one study increased successful ECV among nulliparous but not multiparous women.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 small trials of regional anesthesia vs. intravenous analgesia or no treatment during ECV for breech presentation at term concluded that regional anesthesia was more likely to result in success (60% vs. 38%; RR 1.58; 95% CI, 1.29-1.93; number needed to treat [NNT] = 5). Authors of a Cochrane review found similar results but no differences in cephalic presentation in labor or in cesarean sections.

Planned cesarean section for a term singleton breech infant, prior to labor reduces short-term perinatal or neonatal mortality (RR 0.29; 95% CI, 0.10-0.86, three studies), but at 2 years there was no difference in rates of combined death or developmental delay.

In the single study conducted in a setting with a low national perinatal mortality rate, perinatal or neonatal death (excluding fatal anomalies) or severe neonatal morbidity was reduced with a policy of planned caesarean section (RR 0.07; 95% CI, 0.02-0.29). There were more infants who had been allocated to planned cesarean delivery who had medical problems at two years (RR 1.41; 95% CI, 1.05-1.89, one study). NNT = 100 to prevent one case of neonatal mortality. NNT = 42 to prevent serious neonatal morbidity in the US.

Based on Denmark’s National Birth Registry data, the observed increase in cesarean sections for breech presentation from 79.4% to 94.2% was associated with a reduction in intrapartum and early neonatal deaths and neonatal intensive care unit admissions. Similarly, in a Canadian population-based study of 52,671 breech deliveries, composite neonatal mortality and morbidity rates at 37 weeks gestation or greater were significantly higher after vaginal delivery than after cesarean delivery without labor (adjusted rate ratio 3.60, 95% CI, 2.50-5.15 and adjusted rate difference 15.8/1,000 deliveries, 95% CI, 9.2-25.2). Neonatal mortality and morbidity rates were also higher after cesarean delivery in labor.

In a population study in Norway with 30,861 singleton term breech deliveries, there was no significant difference in perinatal death (8 in the planned vaginal vs. 4 in the planned cesarean group), but neonatal morbidity outcomes including neonatal intensive care unit stays ≥4 days, respiratory morbidity, and intracranial bleeding disorders were significantly worse for planned vaginal deliveries.

In a case series from University Hospital in Norway, however, where 83% of the 750 women with breech presentations were selected for vaginal delivery, there were no significant differences between breech and vertex deliveries in perinatal mortality (OR 1.8; 95% CI, 0.2-15), cord metabolic acidosis (OR 0.8; 95% CI, 0.2-3.2) and moderate or severe neonatal encephalopathy (OR 1.8; 95% CI, 0.5-6.2). Operator skill and staff preparation/comfort may be influencing factors.
There is a small but significant decrease in subsequent neonatal hip dysplasia for breech infants delivered by cesarean section vs. vaginally (5.95% vs. 6.88% [RR 0.87; 95% CI, 0.78-0.97]).

Mothers undergoing cesarean section for breech presentation reported more abdominal pain (RR 1.89; 95% CI, 1.29-2.79), but less incontinence (RR .62; 95% CI, .41-.93) and less perineal pain (RR .32; 95% CI, .18-.58) at 3 months post partum. However, at 2 years maternal outcomes were no different.

A prospective cohort study in France in 2011 with 390 women studied whether a planned route of delivery was associated with perinatal and 2 year neonatal outcomes in preterm infants 26-34 weeks gestational age. The investigators found no association between planned cesarean delivery and improved outcomes for preterm breech singletons compared to planned vaginal deliveries.

With the addition of 6 new trials, moxibustion—burning the Chinese herb Zhiin close to the skin at the lateral fifth metatarsal acupuncture point BL57—does not appear to reduce the need for ECV, although it does reduce the need for oxytocin during labor for women with vaginal deliveries (RR 0.28; 95% CI, 0.13-0.60). Combined with acupuncture or postural technique, moxibustion resulted in fewer non-cephalic presentations at birth and, with acupuncture, fewer caesarean sections compared with no treatment.
Other systematic reviews found moxibustion use at 33 weeks had a positive effect on promoting version of infants in breech presentation that persisted until delivery (NNT = 3.7).

In the most recent RCT of 406 low-risk pregnant women with a breech fetus, women randomize to moxibustion vs. sham moxibustion or usual care were significantly more likely to be in cephalic presentation at term (58.1% vs. 43.4% and 29.7%, respectively).

Acupuncture with fire needling on acupoint BL67 did not result in more successful ECV compared to sham treatment in an RCT of 259 patients between 32 and 34 weeks of gestation (37.7% vs. 28.7% [RR 1.34; 95% CI, 0.93-1.89]).
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends offering an ECV attempt to women near term with breech presentations if there are no contraindications.

ECV at 37 weeks' gestation decreases the rate of noncephalic presentation at birth (RR 0.42; 95% CI, 0.29-0.61) and cesarean delivery (RR 0.57; 95% CI, 0.44-0.82) compared to no attempt at ECV, based on 8 trials. The level of evidence for all trials was low.

In a retrospective database study of 4117 women who had fetal malpresentation at near term, there were no differences between the 31% of women who underwent ECV compared to women who did not undergo the procedure in a composite endpoint for fetal morbidity and mortality (2.9% vs. 2.5%) or neonatal intensive care admission or neonatal anemia. There was a significant reduction in cesarean delivery rates (66% vs. 99%) and 1.8% of the women who attempted ECV underwent cesarean delivery at the time of the procedure for non-reassuring fetal status.

Authors of a meta-analysis found that ECV success rate is similar between women with prior cesarean birth (74%) compared to those without (69%). After a successful ECV, however, the rate of successful vaginal delivery was lower at 75% for women with prior cesarean birth compared to 92% for women without prior cesarean birth.

ECV begun at 34 to 35 weeks may be more effective in reducing noncephalic presentation at the time of labor and therefore cesarean delivery rates than ECV at term. A RCT of 1543 women confirmed that ECV at 34 to 35 weeks vs. at or after 37 weeks resulted in fewer fetuses in a noncephalic presentation at birth (41.1% vs. 49.1%); there were no differences in rates of caesarean section or in risk of preterm birth.

World-wide ECV success rates vary between 36% to 89% with African American and multiparous women having higher success rates than non-African populations and nulliparous women. Success rates in the US and Europe are 36% to 68%. In a meta-analysis of 84 studies, the pooled success rate was 58%.

In a meta-analysis of 53 studies on ECV, factors associated with successful version included multiparity, nonengagement of the breech, a relaxed uterus, a palpable fetal head, and a maternal weight of less than 65 kg. In addition to multiparity, additional success factors from a study of 310 women were increasing estimated fetal weight and normal amniotic fluid. Predictive factors from a study of 500 women were parity of 2, a posterior placenta, and double footling vs. frank breech presentation.

Authors of a Cochrane review of interventions helping to turn babies to vertex during ECV found that parenteral beta stimulants were effective in facilitating successful ECV, increasing cephalic presentation in labor, and reducing caesarean section rate, but safety could not be assessed. Regional analgesia in combination with a tocolytic was more effective than a tocolytic alone for increasing successful versions but had no influence on other outcomes; data quality was low and power insufficient for these outcomes. Data were also insufficient to assess potential benefits from calcium channel blockers and nitric acid donors, regional analgesia without tocolysis, vibroacoustic stimulation, amnioinfusion, systemic opioids and hypnosis, and use of talcum powder or gel to assist ECV. ACOG recommends use of parenteral tocolysis for ECV.

Authors of a recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 trials and 1 quasi-randomized trial including 2296 women with term breech presentations found neuraxial anesthesia (eg, spinal anesthesia) had an approximately 2 to 2.5-fold higher ECV success rate compared to control, intravenous anesthesia or inhalation anesthesia; however, the odds of maternal hypotension increased significantly (OR 9.33; 95% CI, 3.14-27.68).

Inhaled nitrous oxide vs. medical air did not improve overall ECV success rate (24.3% vs. 19.7%) in one RCT of 150 women with singleton breech presentations, but among the 68 parous women, nitrous oxide improved ECV success (47.1% vs. 23.5%). Success rates in this trial are lower than usually reported.

Administration of remifentanil (0.1 μg kg min infusion with demand boluses of 0.1 μg/kg) vs. placebo reduced pain associated with ECV and increased successful version (56.9% vs. placebo group 38.9%) in an RCT of 144 nulliparous women with singleton breech presentation.

In another RCT of 830 women with a singleton fetus in breech presentation, the beta-blocker fenoterol was more successful than the oxytocin receptor antagonist atosiban for ECV (40% vs. 34%) but there was no difference in cephalic presentation at delivery or rates of cesarean delivery (55% vs. 60%).

In a three-armed RCT of 189 women, use of spinal anesthesia increased ECV success rate and reduced pain for both primary and re-attempts of ECV over either intravenous analgesia using remifentanil or no anesthesia (ECV success 83%, 64%, and 64%, respectively).

strong.em: aindications and factors associated with failure of ECV or no benefit

list.listitem: Contraindications for ECV vary between guidelines, but all list oligohydramnios.
In a prospective study, higher thyroid stimulating hormone, nulliparity, frank breech presentation and placenta anterior were associated with ECV failure.
Amniotic fluid index (AFI) less than 10 may correlate with lower success rates for ECV.
Maternal intravenous fluid therapy with 2 L of hypotonic saline prior to ECV appears to increase the amniotic fluid index but does not increase the success rate of the procedure.

Prior cesarean section does not decrease the success rate of ECV but it is not known if there is an increased rate of uterine rupture. A prospective cohort study showed that ECV enabled a vaginal birth in only about a third of women with a history of prior cesarean section.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend postural management for breech presentation with or without ECV.

Approximately 1% of infants undergoing ECV had changes in fetal heart rate requiring immediate delivery. In the same metaanalysis above, there were 49 cases with complications leading to emergency cesarean delivery (0.35%); serious complications (ie, placental abruption and stillbirth) occurred in 23 cases (pooled risk of .24% [95% CI, .17-.34]). Of 12 fetal deaths, 2 were attributed to the procedure.

Planned vaginal delivery may be appropriate in selected patients using set criteria: gestational age more than 37 weeks, frank or complete breech presentation, no fetal anomalies on ultrasound, adequate AFI (>3 cm vertical pocket), adequate maternal pelvis, and estimated fetal weight between 2500 and 4000 g. Similar criteria were published by the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada.
In the case of vaginal breech delivery, capability for immediate cesarean section should be established early and informed consent obtained for both vaginal breech delivery and cesarean section.
Two providers capable of performing the breech delivery should be available as well as a pediatrician for care of the infant and piper forceps in the case of head entrapment.
Although complications of ECV are rare, they can be life threatening. Therefore, it is recommended that access to cesarean section be readily available.
In vaginal breech delivery, active labor positions should be encouraged.
Delivery of the lower extremities, abdomen, and thorax should occur by maternal effort, not traction ().
With delivery of the buttock, abdomen, and thorax, the provider should keep the infants' back anterior.
Arms should be delivered one at a time by turning the shoulder anteriorly and then sweeping the arm in front of and across the chest to promote delivery.
Head flexion can be maintained by pressure on the fetal maxilla, gentle downward traction, and suprapubic pressure if needed.
Adverse maternal and fetal outcomes of both ECV and persistent breech presentation are rare. B
Spontaneous version rate is 40% for multiparous versus 18% for primiparous women. B

Infants who underwent a vaginal breech delivery or delivery by cesarean delivery in labor were more likely to have low 5-minute Apgar scores (OR 6.5; 95% CI, 2.6-16.2) and admission to the neonatal intensive care unit (OR 2.5; 95% CI, 1.2-5.2) than those delivered by planned cesarean delivery prior to labor. There was no significant difference in rate of birth trauma, long-term morbidity, or incidence of neurodevelopmental delay. B
In a large Norwegian birth registry, the OR for cerebral palsy was 3.6 (95% CI, 2.4-5.3) among children born in breech position. B
Breech delivery and children born after successful ECV appear to have an increased risk of developmental hip dysplasia. B
There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine cesarean section for a second twin in breech presentation.
